## Narrative

The honesty lesson, and the one that most directly closes the translation gap: engineers who can say what an LLM *can't* do are the ones clients trust. The misconception to kill: caveats lose deals. The capability to install: a failure taxonomy backed by real public post-mortems, "measured quality, not vibes" as the answer to "how do you know it works?", and sentence patterns that survive contact with production. Caps the module before ASM-2.

| # | Task | Time | Artifact to bring |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Read post-mortem 1: **Moffatt v. Air Canada** (BC Civil Resolution Tribunal, Feb 2024). Air Canada's website chatbot invented a retroactive bereavement-refund policy contradicting the page it linked to; Air Canada argued the chatbot was "a separate legal entity responsible for its own actions"; the tribunal found negligent misrepresentation and awarded CAD $812.02. Coverage: [CBC News](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/air-canada-chatbot-lawsuit-1.7116416) | 15 min | One sentence: "the promise that broke" |
| 2 | Read post-mortem 2: **Mata v. Avianca** (S.D.N.Y., June 2023). Lawyers filed a brief citing six nonexistent cases generated by ChatGPT — then asked ChatGPT to confirm the cases were real, and it vouched for itself. Judge Castel sanctioned the lawyers and firm $5,000 and ordered corrective letters. Overview: [Wikipedia — Mata v. Avianca, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mata_v._Avianca,_Inc.) | 15 min | One sentence: "the promise that broke" |
| 3 | Read post-mortem 3: **indirect prompt injection** — a case where instructions hidden in content the model *retrieved* (a web page, an uploaded document, an email) redirected its behaviour. Curated write-up in the GAP-7 pack; Karpathy's LSN-2.1 pre-work talk closes on this same class of attack | 20 min | One sentence: where the untrusted text entered the system |
| 4 | Read the **privacy / data-boundary one-pager** (GAP-7): client data pasted into consumer tools, and what a boundary drawn by design rather than by policy memo looks like | 15 min | One line: the riskiest paste you've personally seen or nearly made |
| 5 | **Run one injection test yourself.** Put a hidden instruction inside a document (white text, a footnote, an HTML comment — something a human skims past) telling the model to ignore its task and do something else. Paste the document into an LLM under a normal-looking task. Does it obey? Try two variants | 25 min | Your document, the model's response, and your verdict on whether you'd have spotted it as a reviewer |

**Time accounting (pre-work):** 15 + 15 + 20 + 15 + 25 = 90 min.

## Session Plan

| Segment | Time | Method | Detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| Failure taxonomy — one real example each | 25 min | discussion-led | Every row now arrives pre-read, so this segment argues rather than narrates. **Hallucination:** pre-work cases 1–2 — you own what your bot says (Air Canada), and the model is not its own verifier (Avianca). **Staleness:** the reversed-decision demo from the 2.4 lab — confident answers from an outdated corpus. **Prompt injection (awareness level):** pre-work case 3 plus **their own injection tests from task 5, collected and compared** — whose obeyed, whose didn't, who would have caught it in review. Defenses are MOD-3 territory; recognition is today's job. **Privacy leaks:** pre-work case 4; the rule is data boundaries by design, not by policy memo. |
| "How do you know it works?" | 20 min | talk + discussion | Evals at a glance: a golden question set, pass criteria, measure before/after every change. Participants already ran their first eval without naming it — the 2.4 homework's retrieval-quality paragraph — and they are about to build a real one for homework. Promise *measured* quality: "87 of 100 on your test set" beats "it's really good". Brief the homework eval set here so the spec is unambiguous. Deep treatment lands in MOD-3 (production concerns). |
| Drill: rewrite the overpromise | 15 min | drill | Pairs rewrite the three statements below into survivable versions; compare against the reference rewrites; debrief what each rewrite adds (a number, a mechanism, an escalation path). Participants also have their own client sentences from LSN-2.1/2.2/2.3 homework to test against the same bar. |

**Timing check:** 25 + 20 + 15 = 60 min = 1 h — matches the spreadsheet contract.

The live hour was already on contract and is unchanged. All of this lesson's re-scoping went into the out-of-session budget, which grew from 30 min to 4 h.

**The three overpromising statements and reference "survivable" rewrites:**
1. *"It will always answer correctly — it's trained on your documentation."* → "It answers from your documentation and cites the passage it used. We measure accuracy on a test set built from your real questions, and it's designed to say 'not found' rather than guess."
2. *"Because it uses RAG, it can't hallucinate."* → "Retrieval grounds answers in your documents, which sharply reduces fabricated answers — it doesn't eliminate them. Users see the source for every answer, and we track the fabrication rate on an eval set so you see a number, not our word."
3. *"You can cut the support team — the bot handles everything from day one."* → "In a four-week pilot we measure what share of tier-1 tickets it resolves end-to-end; everything below the confidence bar escalates to your team with full context. You staff on the measured deflection rate, not a promise."

## Client Tie-In (Dorel's rule)

Pre-sales scenario, played straight: the construction-site prospect asks "so it'll answer anything about our safety manuals correctly, right?" The survivable version of that answer — grounded, cited, measured, with an escalation path — is the differentiator, and Air Canada is the two-minute story of what the alternative costs. The in-production meeting-RAG system is the honest exemplar: we can show its eval numbers and show it saying "not found."

## Homework

Checkpoint week, but not an empty one: this is where "measured quality, not vibes" stops being a slogan. Task 1 is the module's capstone — the first time a participant produces a **number** for a system they built.

| # | Task | Time | Deliverable |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Build a golden eval set** against your LSN-2.4 RAG pipeline and corpus: 20 questions — 15 answerable from the corpus with the expected answer written down, and **5 deliberately unanswerable**, where the correct behaviour is "not found". Run all 20, score them, and report the number the way you'd report it to a client. Note every case where it confabulated instead of declining | 60 min | The 20-question set with expected answers, your scored results, and your headline number |
| 2 | **Rewrite five overpromises of your own.** Pull five sentences from your own past decks, proposals or emails (or the provided set if you have none) and rewrite each into a survivable version. Every rewrite must add all three: a number, a mechanism, and an escalation path | 30 min | Five before/after pairs, annotated with which of the three each addition supplies |
| 3 | **ASM-2 whiteboard rehearsal, timed and cold.** Sketch a RAG architecture for a given client scenario in 10 minutes without notes, then do it again with a second scenario. After each, write the two design choices you would defend and the one you'd expect to be challenged on | 30 min | Two photographed sketches + your defended choices |
| 4 | **Module self-check.** Work OUT-2.1 through OUT-2.6 and write the honest two-sentence answer for each, as if a client asked. Flag anything you cannot answer without looking it up — those flags go to Tyler **before** ASM-2, not after | 30 min | Six answers + your flagged list, submitted referencing `LSN-2.6` |

ASM-2 (quiz + whiteboard) verifies OUT-2.1–OUT-2.6; this lesson's taxonomy and sentence patterns appear directly in the quiz scenarios, and task 3 is the whiteboard exercise rehearsed under time.

**Time accounting:** pre-work 90 min + homework 150 min = 4 h out-of-session budget.

**Dependency flag:** homework task 1 requires each participant's LSN-2.4 pipeline to still run. Called out in the LSN-2.4 homework too — if a participant's pipeline is dead, the fallback is the provided reference pipeline plus the meeting-notes corpus, which measures the same skill.
